blocks.text: Among all possible motions of material bodies, circular motion is the one that appears to be at work in most of the natural world: satellites moving in circular orbits around the Earth, the orbital and spin motion of the Earth itself, a car turning around a curved road, and a stone whirled around by a string are familiar examples. When objects move in circular paths their direction is continuously changing; since velocity is a vector quantity, this change of direction means that their velocities are not constant. This chapter studies circular motion, rotational motion, moment of inertia, angular momentum and related topics.

blocks.title: The radian
blocks.text: Consider an angle drawn at the centre O of a circle by an arc AB (Fig. 3.1). If the length of the arc AB is equal to the radius r of the circle, the angle is called one radian. It is the SI unit of angular measurement and its symbol is rad.

Consider a single particle P of mass m moving in a circular path of radius r, attached to the end of a massless rigid rod of length r whose other end is pivoted at the centre O (Fig. 3.2a). As the particle moves on the circle the rod OP rotates in the plane of the circle; the axis of rotation passes through the pivot O and is normal to the plane of rotation. Take the z-axis along the axis of rotation with O as origin, and the x- and y-axes in the plane of rotation (Fig. 3.2b). At an instant t let the position of OP be OP1, making angle theta with the x-axis; at a later time t + delta t let it be OP2, making angle theta + delta theta (Fig. 3.2c).

blocks.title: Angular displacement
blocks.text: The angle delta theta defines the angular displacement of OP during the time interval delta t. For very small values of delta theta the angular displacement is a vector quantity. It is assigned a positive sign when the sense of rotation of OP is counter-clockwise. Its direction is along the axis of rotation and is given by the right-hand rule (Fig. 3.2d): grasp the axis of rotation in the right hand with the fingers curling in the direction of rotation; the thumb points in the direction of the angular displacement.

Three units are generally used for angular displacement: degrees, revolution and radian. For an arc of length S of a circle of radius r (Fig. 3.3) subtending angle theta at the centre, its value in radians is theta = S/r, or S = r theta (where theta is in radian) ... (3.1). If OP rotates, the point P covers a distance S = 2 pi r in one revolution, which in radians is S/r = 2 pi r / r = 2 pi; so 1 revolution = 2 pi rad = 360 degrees, or 1 rad = 360/(2 pi) = 57.3 degrees.

blocks.caption: Angular measurements: radian, angular displacement, velocity and acceleration (original diagram after Figures 3.1 to 3.5 and topic 3.1).
blocks.long_description: An arc equal in length to the radius subtends one radian at the centre, so an angle in radians is the arc divided by the radius and a full revolution is two pi radians. A rod pivoted at the centre and turning through a small angle in a short time has that angle as its angular displacement, taken positive counter-clockwise and directed along the axis by the right-hand rule. Angular velocity is the rate of angular displacement and angular acceleration the rate of change of angular velocity, both along the axis. A point at distance r from the axis moves along the tangent with speed r times the angular velocity and has tangential acceleration r times the angular acceleration, so the equations of linear motion carry over to angular motion with angle, angular velocity and angular acceleration in place of displacement, velocity and acceleration, provided the axis is fixed.

blocks.text: Very often we want to know how fast or how slow a body is rotating; this is determined by its angular velocity, the rate at which the angular displacement changes with time. Referring to Fig. 3.2c, if delta theta is the angular displacement during the time interval delta t, the average angular velocity during the interval is omega_av = delta theta / delta t ... (3.2). The instantaneous angular velocity omega is the limit of the ratio delta theta / delta t as delta t approaches zero: omega = lim (delta t -> 0) delta theta / delta t ... (3.3). In this limit the angular displacement is infinitesimally small, so it is a vector quantity and the angular velocity defined by Eq. 3.3 is also a vector, directed along the axis of rotation by the right-hand rule. Angular velocity is measured in radians per second, the SI unit; sometimes it is given in revolutions per minute (rpm).

When we switch on an electric fan its angular velocity goes on increasing: it has an angular acceleration, defined as the rate of change of angular velocity. If omega_i and omega_f are the instantaneous angular velocities of a rotating body at instants t_i and t_f, the average angular acceleration during the interval t_f - t_i is alpha_av = (omega_f - omega_i)/(t_f - t_i) = delta omega / delta t ... (3.4). The instantaneous angular acceleration is the limit of the ratio delta omega / delta t as delta t approaches zero: alpha = lim (delta t -> 0) delta omega / delta t ... (3.5). Angular acceleration is also a vector, with magnitude given by Eq. 3.5 and direction along the axis of rotation; it is expressed in rad s^-2.

So far we have considered a particle P fixed at the end of a rotating massless rod. Now consider the rotation of a rigid body (Fig. 3.4): imagine a point P on the body and let OP be the perpendicular dropped from P on the axis of rotation, called the reference line. As the body rotates, OP also rotates with the same angular velocity and angular acceleration, so the rotation of a rigid body is described by the rotation of its reference line, and all the terms defined with the rotating line OP are valid for the rotational motion of a rigid body.
Relation between angular and linear velocities

Consider a rigid body rotating about the z-axis with angular velocity omega (Fig. 3.5a), and a point P in the body at perpendicular distance r from the axis, OP being the reference line. As the body rotates, P moves along a circle of radius r with linear velocity v while OP rotates with angular velocity omega (Fig. 3.5b). Since the axis is fixed, the direction of omega always remains the same and omega can be manipulated as a scalar; for the linear velocity of P we consider its magnitude only, also treated as a scalar. Suppose P moves through a distance P1P2 = delta S in time delta t while OP covers an angular displacement delta theta radian; by Eq. 3.1, delta S = r delta theta. Dividing both sides by delta t, delta S / delta t = r delta theta / delta t ... (3.6). In the limit delta t -> 0 the ratio delta S / delta t is v, the magnitude of the velocity with which P moves on the circumference, and delta theta / delta t is the angular velocity omega of OP, so v = r omega ... (3.7). In the limit the arc P1P2 becomes very small and its direction is the tangent to the circle at P1: the velocity of P has magnitude v and its direction is always along the tangent at that point, which is why the linear velocity of P is also known as the tangential velocity. Similarly, if OP rotates with angular acceleration alpha, P has a linear or tangential acceleration a_t, and using Eq. 3.7 it can be shown that a_t = r alpha ... (3.8). Equations 3.7 and 3.8 show that on a rotating body points at different distances from the axis do not have the same speed or acceleration, but all points on a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis have the same angular displacement, angular speed and angular acceleration at any instant; so the angular variables describe the motion of the whole body simply. A wheel turning through an angle theta lays out a tangential distance S = r theta (Do You Know).

Equations 3.2 to 3.5 of angular motion are exactly analogous to those of linear motion if theta, omega and alpha replace S, v and a. As the other equations of linear motion were obtained by algebraic manipulation of these equations, analogous equations also apply to angular motion.
The angular equations 3.9 to 3.11 hold true only when the axis of rotation is fixed, so that all the angular vectors have the same direction and can be manipulated as scalars.

blocks.title: Example 3.1
blocks.text: An electric fan rotating at 3 rev s^-1 is switched off and comes to rest in 18.0 s. Assuming the deceleration to be uniform, find its value, and the number of revolutions turned before coming to rest. Solution: omega_i = 3.0 rev s^-1, omega_f = 0, t = 18.0 s, alpha = ?, theta = ?. From Eq. 3.9, alpha = (omega_f - omega_i)/t = (0 - 3.0) rev s^-1 / 18.0 s = -0.167 rev s^-2. From Eq. 3.11, theta = omega_i t + (1/2) alpha t^2 = 3.0 rev s^-1 x 18.0 s + (1/2)(-0.167 rev s^-2)(18.0 s)^2 = 27 rev.

blocks.prompt: A car moving at 108 km h^-1 has wheels of diameter 60 cm; find the angular speed of a wheel in rad s^-1 and rev s^-1. An electric motor at 1800 rev min^-1 is switched off and stops uniformly in 20 s; how many revolutions does it make (numerical problems 3.2, 3.3)?
blocks.explanation: v = 108 km h^-1 = 30 m s^-1 and r = 0.30 m, so omega = v/r = 100 rad s^-1 = 100/(2 pi) = 16 rev s^-1. For the motor omega_i = 1800 rev min^-1 = 30 rev s^-1, omega_f = 0, t = 20 s: alpha = -30/20 = -1.5 rev s^-2 and theta = 30 x 20 + (1/2)(-1.5)(400) = 600 - 300 = 300 rev.

items: 1 rad: arc = radius; theta = S/r, S = r theta; 1 rev = 2 pi rad = 360 degrees, 1 rad = 57.3 degrees. Angular displacement delta theta is a vector (small angles), positive counter-clockwise, direction by the right-hand rule along the axis.

omega = delta theta / delta t (rad s^-1, rpm), alpha = delta omega / delta t (rad s^-2), both along the axis; v = r omega, a_t = r alpha; velocity is along the tangent. Angular equations: omega_f = omega_i + alpha t; 2 alpha theta = omega_f^2 - omega_i^2; theta = omega_i t + (1/2) alpha t^2, for a fixed axis. Example 3.1: -0.167 rev s^-2, 27 rev.
